verses.text: Then the battle turned; until then, both sides had held their ground,
fighting steadfastly through the fierce clashes.
At the front, Cottus, Briareus, and Gyges stirred up savage battle,
warriors who could never have their fill of war.
From their powerful hands they hurled three hundred rocks
in quick succession, overshadowing with their missiles
the Titans, whom they sent beneath the earth with its wide roads
and bound in painful chains,
overpowering them with their hands, proud though the Titans were,
as far beneath the earth as the sky is above it.
That is how far it is from earth to misty Tartarus.
For nine nights and nine days a bronze anvil
falling from the sky would reach the earth on the tenth day;
and again, for nine nights and nine days a bronze anvil
falling from earth would reach Tartarus on the tenth.
A bronze fence surrounds Tartarus, and Night
spreads in three layers around its neck, while above it
grow the roots of earth and the sea that yields no harvest.
There the Titan gods lie hidden in misty darkness,
by the will of Zeus, the cloud-gatherer,
in a dank place at the ends of the vast earth.
They cannot get out. Poseidon has fitted doors
of bronze across the entrance, and a wall runs around on either side.
There Gyges, Cottus, and great-hearted Obriareus
live as faithful guards of Zeus, who carries the aegis.
There, of dark earth and misty Tartarus,
of the sea that yields no harvest and the starry sky,
the sources and boundaries all lie side by side,
dreadful, dank places that even the gods hate.
There is a huge chasm: even in a whole year
you would not reach its floor, once you had passed inside its gates.
Instead, storm after storm would carry you this way and that,
savage storms. Even the immortal gods find terrifying
this marvel. There stands the fearsome house of dark Night,
wrapped in blue-black clouds.
Before it, Iapetus's son holds up the broad sky,
standing with his head and tireless hands supporting it,
unshaken. Here Night and Day draw near
and greet each other as they cross the great threshold
of bronze. One goes inside while the other
goes out; the house never holds them both at once.
One is always outside the house,
travelling over the earth, while the other stays inside
and waits until her own time to set out arrives.
Day brings people on earth the light that lets them see far,
while Night holds Sleep in her hands, the brother of Death,
deadly Night, wrapped in a misty cloud.
There the children of dark Night have their homes,
Sleep and Death, fearsome gods. Never does
shining Helios, the Sun, look upon them with his rays,
either as he climbs into the sky or as he comes down from it.
Sleep travels over the earth and the broad back of the sea,
peaceful and gentle toward human beings.
But Death has a heart of iron, and a heart of bronze
lies merciless within his chest; he holds on to whoever he first seizes
among humankind. Even the immortal gods hate him.
There, in front, stand the echoing halls of the god below,
mighty Hades, and of dreaded Persephone.
A fearsome dog keeps watch before them,
merciless, with a cruel trick: as people enter,
he greets them all with wagging tail and both ears,
but never lets them back out. Instead, he lies in wait
and devours anyone he catches going outside the gates
of mighty Hades and dreaded Persephone.

uncertainties: Verse 774 is marked for deletion in the supplied Greek. It is translated here because it is among the assigned verses.
The precise image of Night spreading in three layers around Tartarus's 'neck' in verses 726–727 is unclear; the translation preserves it.
